title: Matrix Function Reduction Overview
content:
The Cayley-Hamilton theorem implies that any polynomial function of an n*n matrix A can be reduced to a polynomial of degree at most n-1. This file proves that reduction theorem and its consequences.

The key equation: aeval A p = aeval A (p mod charpoly(A)). This means computing p(A) for any polynomial p only requires knowing I, A, ..., A^{n-1}.
mathContext: Foundation for computing matrix exponentials, powers, and other matrix functions efficiently.

title: The Polynomial Reduction Theorem
content:
**Theorem** (aeval_eq_aeval_modByMonic): For any polynomial f and matrix A,
  aeval A f = aeval A (f mod charpoly(A))

**Proof**: By the division algorithm, f = q * charpoly(A) + r. Evaluating at A: f(A) = q(A) * 0 + r(A) = r(A), since charpoly(A) annihilates A by Cayley-Hamilton.
mathContext: This is the core algebraic result. The characteristic polynomial acts as a modular reduction operator for matrix polynomial evaluation.

title: Degree Bound: Reduced Polynomial Has Degree < n
content:
**Theorem** (degree_reduced_lt_dim): The remainder f mod charpoly(A) has natDegree < Fintype.card n.

Since charpoly has degree exactly n (by charpoly_natDegree_eq_dim), and the remainder of division by a monic polynomial has strictly smaller degree, any polynomial expression in A reduces to a linear combination of I, A, ..., A^{n-1}.
mathContext: This bounds the dimension of the algebra generated by A to at most n, matching the matrix dimension.

title: Power Reduction
content:
**Theorem** (power_eq_aeval_mod): A^k = aeval A (X^k mod charpoly(A)).

This is the specialization of the reduction theorem to monomials X^k. For k >= n, the power A^k is a linear combination of lower powers. For example, with a 3x3 matrix, A^100 reduces to c_0*I + c_1*A + c_2*A^2.
mathContext: The practical payoff: computing high matrix powers requires only polynomial arithmetic modulo a degree-n polynomial.

title: Congruence Theorem
content:
**Theorem** (congruence): If f mod charpoly(A) = g mod charpoly(A), then aeval A f = aeval A g.

This says the evaluation map factors through the quotient ring R[X]/(charpoly), which has dimension n as an R-module. Two polynomials that are 'equivalent modulo charpoly' give the same matrix.
mathContext: The quotient ring R[X]/(charpoly) is the abstract algebra capturing all polynomial functions of A.

title: Annihilator Ideal Structure
content:
**Theorems**: The set of polynomials p with aeval A p = 0 forms an ideal:
- Closed under addition (annihilator_add)
- Closed under left multiplication (annihilator_mul_left)
- Contains all multiples of charpoly (charpoly_multiple_annihilates)

This ideal is generated by the minimal polynomial, which divides the characteristic polynomial.
mathContext: The annihilator ideal is the kernel of the evaluation homomorphism R[X] -> M_n(R).

title: Partial Sum Reduction for Matrix Exponentials
content:
**Theorem** (partial_sum_reduces): Any finite partial sum sum_{k<N} c_k * X^k, when evaluated at A, equals the evaluation of the reduced partial sum.

This is the key algebraic step for computing matrix exponentials. The series exp(tA) = sum (tA)^k/k! can be reduced term by term, giving exp(tA) = c_0(t)*I + c_1(t)*A + ... + c_{n-1}(t)*A^{n-1}.
mathContext: Connects the algebraic reduction to analysis: power series partial sums reduce via charpoly, enabling matrix exponential computation.

title: Nilpotent Matrix Characterization
content:
**Theorem** (nilpotent_from_charpoly): If charpoly(A) = X^n, then A^n = 0.

For nilpotent matrices, the matrix exponential truncates exactly: exp(A) = I + A + A^2/2! + ... + A^{n-1}/(n-1)! since all higher terms vanish.
mathContext: Nilpotent matrices are the simplest case where Cayley-Hamilton gives explicit vanishing of powers.

title: Idempotent Power Theorem
content:
**Theorem** (idempotent_power): If A^2 = A, then A^k = A for all k > 0.

For idempotent matrices, the matrix exponential becomes: exp(tA) = I + (e^t - 1)*A. All the complexity of the exponential series collapses to a single coefficient.
mathContext: Idempotent matrices are projections. Their spectral decomposition is trivially A = P where P projects onto the range.
